ledger.note: 1351: Zou Pusheng takes Qishui in southern Hubei and enthrones Xu Shouhui as emperor of Tianwan. Red Turban Rebellions page: 1351 (September): Zou Pusheng captured Qishui in southern Hubei and enthroned Xu Shouhui as emperor of Tianwan; the Tianwan page says the rising began in August-September 1351 and names Qizhou, the Chen Han page says 'eastern Hubei' in August 1351.

region.text: Hanyang and Wuchang on the Yangtze (the Wuhan cities)

ledger.note: 1352: Tianwan seizes Hanyang and Wuchang. 'In the early spring of 1352, he seized Hanyang' and then Wuchang across the Yangtze; the Red Turban page says they were driven off in 1352 (see the 1353 loss).

union.text: Jiujiang on the Yangtze in northern Jiangxi

ledger.note: 1352: Tianwan reaches Jiujiang and takes Nanchang and Changsha. 1352-1353: Tianwan forces advanced to Jiujiang and captured Nanchang and Changsha; the page gives the span, not the year of each city, so 1352 is the first year of the span.

region.text: Qishui (Xishui) in eastern Hubei, where the page says Zou Pusheng and Xu Shouhui rose in 1351 (the Tianwan page says they took Qizhou, modern Qichun, nearby)

ledger.note: 1353: Toqto'a's army takes the Tianwan capital. 'By fall, Toqto'a's forces had captured the Tianwan capital of Qishui'; Xu escaped, about 400 officials died and the court hid in the mountains of Huangmei County.

Jiujiang on the Yangtze in northern Jiangxi

ledger.note: 1353: the Yangtze and Jiangxi cities are lost with the capital. The page is silent on when Hanyang, Jiujiang, Nanchang and Changsha were lost; it says only that Ni Wenjun recaptured Hanyang in January 1355, so the map reduces Tianwan to the Huangmei refuge in 1354 (confidence 1, a gap for a gap-filler). The Red Turban page has Tianwan driven off Hanyang, Hankou and Wuchang already in 1352, so the loss of the Wuhan cities may be a year earlier.

Winter 1355/56: Xu Shouhui moves the court to Hanyang. 'In the winter of 1355/56, Xu moved to Hanyang' (the infobox dates Hanyang from 1353).

ledger.note: 1357: Ming Yuzhen conquers Sichuan in Xu Shouhui's name. Ming Yuzhen led 10,000 men up the Yangtze into Sichuan. Upon conquering Sichuan, Ming assumed virtual autonomy and ruled in the name of Xu Shouhui. Drawn as a vassal tint until 1360.

ledger.note: 1360: Ming Yuzhen takes the title of king of Longshu in Sichuan after Xu's murder. The Tianwan page lists Ming Yuzhen declared himself king of Longshu in Sichuan among the successors; the Ming Xia page gives both 1360 and 1362 for the title.

notes: Written for ea-06-x from three pages (Tianwan (Xu Shouhui), Red Turban Rebellions, Chen Han); Cliopatria has no Tianwan row, so every keyframe is new and every shape is a city-circle or province union, not a surveyed outline. Disagreements: the Red Turban page and the Chen Han page say Qishui/eastern Hubei, the Tianwan page says Qizhou; the Tianwan infobox dates Hanyang as capital from 1353 but its text says the winter of 1355/56 (and in 1353-55 the court hid in Huangmei); the Tianwan page puts Ni Wenjun's January 1355 conquest at Mianyang in Sichuan, which is probably the Mianyang near Xiantao in Hubei (a reading from outside the page; a gap-filler should check) and is not mapped. The Red Turban page also says the state took Chongqing and held all of Sichuan under Chen Youliang in 1357-1359; the Tianwan and Ming Xia pages give Sichuan to Ming Yuzhen in 1357, and this dossier follows them. The dates of the loss of the Yangtze cities in 1353-55 and the territory in Shaanxi are not on any page opened. Names for the gazetteer: Qishui (Xishui), Qizhou (Qichun), Huangmei refuge is a circle by coordinate. Counterparts needing dossiers: yuan-dynasty (ea-06-a), chen-han and ming-xia (this batch).
